title: This founder is making cheaper, cleaner steel
gist: Hertha Metals founder Laureen Meroueh has built a single-step furnace that turns iron ore directly into liquid steel using natural gas instead of coal, claiming at least 50% lower emissions and 25% lower costs than conventional blast-furnace steelmaking, and is scaling from a 1-ton/day Texas pilot toward a 10,000-ton/year plant by end-2027 and 500,000 tons/year by 2030 on roughly $20M raised to date.

themes.theme: Steel's decarbonization problem and Hertha's fix

insights.claim: Global steelmaking generates roughly 7% of the carbon emissions driving climate change, comparable to the fashion industry, because the dominant blast-furnace process — largely unchanged since it was commercialized in the 1850s — relies on melting iron ore with coal-derived gases.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: A ~7%-of-global-emissions industry with a 170-year-old dominant process is a large, underserved decarbonization TAM for any founder who can cut costs, not just emissions, since steelmakers' thin margins have historically blocked green retrofits.
insights.quote: It then undergoes further refining to purify it before it is made into products like rebar and car frames. The process relies on coal, and it generates roughly 7% of the carbon emissions that drive climate change—about as much as the fashion industry.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The majority of steelmakers melt solid iron ore'

insights.claim: Steel decarbonization has stalled industry-wide because profit margins are tight and blast furnaces have long service lives, making it economically hard for incumbents to justify capital investment in cleaner processes.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Explains why steel decarbonization is a capital-cycle problem, not just a technology problem — any winning approach must beat incumbents on cost now, not just on emissions, which is exactly Hertha's positioning.
insights.quote: Decarbonization has proved difficult: Profit margins are tight and furnaces have long service lives, making investment tough to justify.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The process relies on coal'

insights.claim: Hertha Metals' furnace turns iron ore into refined liquid steel in a single step (versus the conventional multi-step melt-then-refine process) and substitutes natural gas for coal, which together cut emissions by at least half and reduce costs by 25% compared with standard steelmaking, according to founder Laureen Meroueh.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: A claimed simultaneous cost reduction (not just emissions reduction) is the key commercial differentiator versus hydrogen-based green-steel approaches, which typically raise costs — if verified at scale, this reverses the usual decarbonization cost penalty.
insights.quote: Her method turns iron ore into refined liquid steel in a single step, and it swaps coal for natural gas. Together, those changes slash emissions by at least half, she says, and cut costs by 25% compared with steelmaking business as usual.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Now Laureen Meroueh may have found a way'

insights.claim: Iryna Zenyuk, director of the National Fuel Cell Research Center at UC Irvine, says the value proposition of Hertha's approach lies in shrinking the size and complexity of the production system itself, since blast furnaces are massive, inefficient, and energy-intensive.
insights.speaker: Iryna Zenyuk, National Fuel Cell Research Center, UC Irvine
insights.so_what: Third-party academic validation frames Hertha's edge as process simplification/miniaturization, not just fuel-switching — a defensible technical moat if patentable, distinct from easier-to-copy fuel substitution alone.
insights.quote: There’s huge value in reducing the size of this production system

insights.claim: Hertha deliberately chose a fossil-fuel-based (natural gas) near-term path over hydrogen-based green steel, prioritizing cost control now, but Meroueh says the current plant design could switch to a fully decarbonized system without major hardware changes if and when hydrogen becomes more affordable.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: A hardware-agnostic-to-hydrogen design gives Hertha optionality: it is not making a one-way bet against hydrogen, so its cost-now strategy doesn't foreclose future upside if hydrogen economics improve — reduces technology-obsolescence risk for investors.
insights.quote: The current Hertha plant could eventually switch to a fully decarbonized system without drastically changing the hardware, she says, if hydrogen becomes more affordable.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'While other approaches to making green steel'

insights.claim: Hertha Metals had raised about $20 million in funding as of July 2026, and Khosla Ventures partner Rajesh Swaminathan (an investor in the company) says Hertha's scale-up is impressive given how little the team has spent, contrasting it with competitors that have produced far less steel despite raising $50 million to $100 million.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan, Khosla Ventures
insights.so_what: A capital-efficiency claim from a named institutional investor (2-4x less capital raised than peers for more output) is a concrete comparative data point for benchmarking Hertha against other green-steel startups in follow-on due diligence.
insights.quote: Competitors, he notes, have created far less steel with $50 million or $100 million in funding.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'That facility can produce one metric ton'

insights.claim: Hertha's pilot plant in Conroe, Texas can currently produce one metric ton of steel per day, which Khosla Ventures' Rajesh Swaminathan calls 'a big metric for steel' at this stage.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan, Khosla Ventures
insights.so_what: A concrete current-output baseline (1 ton/day) against which to measure the credibility of Hertha's forward production targets (10,000 tons/year by 2027, 500,000 tons/year by 2030).
insights.quote: That facility can produce one metric ton of steel per day. “One ton per day is a big metric for steel,” says Rajesh Swaminathan, a partner at Khosla Ventures, one of the company’s investors.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'That facility can produce one metric ton'

themes.theme: Scale-up trajectory versus US steel market size

insights.claim: Hertha plans to expand into a new plant adjacent to its existing pilot, targeting 10,000 metric tons of high-purity steel per year at full capacity by the end of 2027, then scaling to 500,000 metric tons per year by 2030 with the addition of a third site.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Gives investors concrete production milestones (10,000 t/yr by end-2027; 500,000 t/yr by 2030) to track Hertha's execution against — a scale-up of roughly 3,650x from the current 1-ton/day pilot in under 4 years is an aggressive but falsifiable target.
insights.quote: The facility is slated to produce 10,000 metric tons of high-purity steel per year and should reach full capacity by the end of 2027. By 2030, Meroueh believes, Hertha can up its output to 500,000 metric tons per year with the addition of a third site.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'In the meantime, plans are underway'

insights.claim: Even Hertha's 2030 target of 500,000 metric tons per year would represent only a fraction of the approximately 80 million metric tons of steel the US produces annually, though Iryna Zenyuk notes that producing even one metric ton with this new process is still an achievement given the industry's scale.
insights.speaker: Bridget Reed Morawski
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable opportunity: even at full projected 2030 scale, Hertha would capture well under 1% of US steel output, underscoring both the market's enormous headroom and the long capital-intensive road to material market share.
insights.quote: That’s only a fraction of the approximately 80 million metric tons of steel produced annually in the US, but Zenyuk says making even one metric ton is still an achievement.
